# Anatomy of a Chapter {#sec-anatomy}

Every chapter in this book follows the same layout, so you always know where to look. This appendix explains each block and then shows one complete solved problem, laid out exactly as it is in the chapters.

```{python}
#| include: false
import random
random.seed(0)
```

## The blocks

| Block | What it holds | How to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Statement** | The problem in a few lines, with constraints | Read the constraints first: they tell you the complexity you need |
| **💡 Intuition** | The one observation that makes the problem easy | Stop here and try to finish the problem yourself |
| **Approach** | Brute force first, then the refined algorithm, with its invariant | Check that you can say why the invariant holds |
| **Code** | Python and C++ in tabs. The Python runs when the book is built and is stress-tested against a brute force | Click a tab to switch languages. Your choice is kept for the whole page |
| **Complexity** | Time and space, with the argument | Say it out loud, as you would in an interview |
| **Edge cases** | Inputs that break naive code | Turn each one into a test |
| **Practice** | Problems that use the same idea, ordered by concept | **CF** = Codeforces (number = rating), **LC** = LeetCode (Easy / Medium / Hard), **CSES**, **AC** = AtCoder |

Codeforces ratings use the Codeforces colours: [grey]{style="color:#808080"} below 1200, [green]{style="color:#16a34a"} 1200–1399, [cyan]{style="color:#0891b2"} 1400–1599, [blue]{style="color:#2563eb"} 1600–1899, [violet]{style="color:#9333ea"} 1900–2099, [orange]{style="color:#ea580c"} 2100–2399, and [red]{style="color:#dc2626"} 2400 and above.

## Pattern: opposite-end two pointers {#sec-anatomy-pattern}

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
On a **sorted** array, put `lo` at the start and `hi` at the end. Look at `a[lo] + a[hi]`: if it is too small, only moving `lo` right can increase it; if it is too large, only moving `hi` left can decrease it. Each step discards one element for good, so the scan is $O(n)$.
:::

### Problem: Pair with a target sum in a sorted array {#sec-anatomy-two-sum-sorted}

::: {.p-statement}
Given a non-decreasing array $a$ of $n$ integers ($2 \le n \le 3\cdot10^4$, $|a_i| \le 1000$) and a target $t$, return 1-based indices $i < j$ with $a_i + a_j = t$. Exactly one answer exists. Use $O(1)$ extra space.

Source: [LC 167 · Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum-ii-input-array-is-sorted/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
If $a_{lo} + a_{hi} < t$, then $a_{lo}$ cannot pair with **any** element, because $a_{hi}$ is the largest one left. So $lo$ can be thrown away. The same argument with the roles swapped throws away $hi$ when the sum is too big.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Brute force.** Try every pair: $O(n^2)$ time. With $n = 3\cdot10^4$ that is $4.5\cdot10^8$ pairs, which is too slow.
2. **Hash map.** One pass storing values seen so far: $O(n)$ time, but $O(n)$ space, and it ignores that the array is sorted.
3. **Two pointers.** Start with $lo = 0$, $hi = n-1$. While $lo < hi$: if the sum equals $t$, return; if it is smaller, `lo += 1`; otherwise `hi -= 1`.

**Invariant.** If the answer is $(i^*, j^*)$, then $lo \le i^*$ and $j^* \le hi$ throughout. A pointer only moves past an index that, by the intuition above, cannot be part of the answer.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
#### Python

```{python}
#| label: anatomy-two-sum
def two_sum_sorted(a: list[int], t: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = a[lo] + a[hi]
        if s == t:
            return lo + 1, hi + 1
        if s < t:
            lo += 1
        else:
            hi -= 1
    raise ValueError("no pair")


def brute(a, t):
    n = len(a)
    return next((i + 1, j + 1) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n) if a[i] + a[j] == t)


# Stress test: random sorted arrays with exactly one valid pair.
for _ in range(2000):
    n = random.randint(2, 12)
    a = sorted(random.randint(-20, 20) for _ in range(n))
    t = random.randint(-40, 40)
    pairs = [(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n) if a[i] + a[j] == t]
    if len(pairs) != 1:
        continue
    assert two_sum_sorted(a, t) == brute(a, t)

assert two_sum_sorted([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == (1, 2)
assert two_sum_sorted([-1, 0], -1) == (1, 2)
assert two_sum_sorted([1, 3, 3, 8], 6) == (2, 3)
print("all tests passed")
```

#### C++

```cpp
vector<int> twoSum(const vector<int>& a, int t) {
    int lo = 0, hi = (int)a.size() - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int s = a[lo] + a[hi];
        if (s == t) return {lo + 1, hi + 1};
        if (s < t) ++lo; else --hi;
    }
    return {};  // unreachable: exactly one answer exists
}
```
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** $O(n)$: each iteration moves one pointer one step inward, and they meet after at most $n-1$ steps. **Space** $O(1)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 2$: the loop runs once.
- Duplicates such as `[1, 3, 3, 8]` with $t = 6$: the answer uses two equal values at different indices, so the condition must be `lo < hi`, not `lo <= hi`.
- Negative numbers: the argument only needs the array to be sorted.
- Overflow: with $|a_i| \le 10^9$ in C++, compute the sum in `long long`.
:::

## Reusing a problem in another chapter {#sec-anatomy-reuse}

Every solved problem is written **once**, in the problem registry (`books/problems/<key>/`), and included in full by its home chapter. When a later chapter needs it again — to compare it with a variant, or to remind the reader of an idea — it includes the problem's **card** instead. This is the card for Climbing Stairs, included here exactly as a chapter would:

{{< include ../problems/lc-0070-climbing-stairs/card.qmd >}}

The card is generated from the problem itself (its title, source and intuition), so it never goes out of date, and its link always points to the one full write-up. A chapter can also include the problem's `solution.qmd` to run the same tested code again.

## How to write a new chapter

```bash
python scripts/new_chapter.py NNN --prefix SLUG --owner me               # from outline.yml + the template; claims the chapter
python scripts/new_problem.py LC 70 "Climbing Stairs" --difficulty Easy  # one registry folder per problem
.venv/Scripts/python scripts/check_chapter.py books/<folder>/NNN_<slug>.qmd   # run every Python cell
.venv/Scripts/python scripts/check_changed.py                            # while editing: only what changed
.venv/Scripts/python scripts/check_style.py books/<folder>/NNN_<slug>.qmd     # structure, hidden figures, PDF-breaking math
.venv/Scripts/python scripts/check_cpp.py books/<folder>/NNN_<slug>.qmd       # compile every C++ tab
.venv/Scripts/python scripts/review_figs.py books/<folder>/NNN_<slug>.qmd     # every figure, light and dark, on one sheet
.venv/Scripts/python scripts/check_links.py --online                     # judge links: id, name, rating
powershell scripts/build.ps1                                             # the website (add -To all for PDF and EPUB)
```

When the checks pass, set `status: written` for the chapter in `outline.yml` and remove its `owner:`.

The build adds the chapter to the sidebar and to its part's opener page, marks it on the home page, generates the cards of its problems, copies its Summary template and Pattern map into the cheat sheets (@sec-cheatsheets) and its interview questions into the question bank (@sec-question-bank), and, for chapters from Part II on, adds its problems to the problem index (@sec-problem-index). Terms added to `glossary.yml` appear in the glossary (@sec-glossary); every diagram type is shown with its code in the gallery (@sec-gallery).
